content: The common cold is a viral infection that affects the upper respiratory tract, also known as an upper respiratory infection (URI). It is caused by various respiratory viruses and typically lasts less than a week. The common cold is one of the most frequent reasons for missed school and work. On average, adults in the United States experience two to three colds per year, while children tend to have even more frequent occurrences. Signs and Symptoms The symptoms of a cold usually reach their peak within two to three days after infection. These symptoms may include: A runny nose or nasal congestion Coughing Sneezing A sore throat Headaches Mild body aches A low-grade fever, which is more common in older children and adults Complications Complications from respiratory virus infections can range from mild to severe. Mild to Moderate Complications: Middle ear infections, which involve infection behind the eardrum Sinus infections Potentially Severe Complications: Asthma exacerbations, which may involve wheezing and difficulty breathing Bronchiolitis, an infection of the small airways in the lungs Bronchitis, an infection of the larger airways Pneumonia, an infection of the lungs Worsening of pre-existing chronic medical conditions, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or heart failure Certain respiratory illnesses, such as COVID-19, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), can lead to serious outcomes, including hospitalization or death. These risks are particularly significant for vulnerable populations, such as infants, older adults, and individuals with underlying medical conditions or weakened immune systems. Causes More than 200 different respiratory viruses are capable of causing the common cold. Rhinoviruses are the most common cause of colds in the United States. Other viruses that can lead to colds include: Common human coronaviruses Parainfluenza viruses Adenoviruses Enteroviruses, including EV-D68 Human metapneumovirus It is important to note that certain viruses, such as SARS-CoV-2 (the virus responsible for COVID-19), influenza viruses, and RSV, can cause symptoms similar to those of a cold but are not classified as causes of the common cold. These viruses are more likely to result in severe illness. If you experience cold-like symptoms and suspect COVID-19 or influenza, it is recommended to get tested, especially if you are at higher risk for severe illness. Antiviral treatments are available for both COVID-19 and influenza, and they are most effective when initiated shortly after symptom onset. Spread Respiratory viruses spread through various mechanisms. Most commonly, they are transmitted via respiratory droplets that are expelled when an infected person coughs or sneezes. These droplets can enter the body when inhaled or when they come into contact with the eyes, nose, or mouth after touching a contaminated surface. Some viruses can also spread through close personal contact, such as shaking hands with an infected individual and then touching your face. Although colds can occur at any time of the year, certain respiratory viruses, such as influenza and RSV, are more prevalent during the winter months. However, other viruses capable of causing cold symptoms may circulate during the spring, summer, or fall. Prevention To reduce the risk of contracting or spreading respiratory viruses, it is important to follow preventive measures. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) provides guidance on how to protect yourself and others from respiratory viruses.
